newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Products Outlook - Heat collapse eyed.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Products Outlook - Heat collapse eyed.

text.p: Demand for U.S. heating oil is likely to remain strong this week and possibly keep a floor beneath cash values but traders say they are predicting a fall-off soon as storage tanks near full capacity.
For the past few weeks, traders have been scooping up big heating oil parcels due to a continuing contango on the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Contango, which when outer-month barrels are more expensive than near-month fuel, allows purchasers to fix their prices and cover storage costs several months ahead of the winter heating season.

"I do not have any (heating oil) buyers in the Gulf. I do not have and buyers in the Caribbean. I can't get anything to the East Coast with shipping costs so high. I think we're kind of stuck," said one Gulf Coast trader.
"Distillates look like they will be ugly going into the fall," one New York trader said.

"This is the first time I've seen spreads of a full penny in two years," he said, noting that October heating oil settled at 53.36 cents a gallon last Friday versus 52.26 cents for September contracts.
Similarly, November heating oil -- at 54.31 cents -- was 0.95 cent more expensive than October fuel.
Meanwhile, traders said they were unsure which direction gasoline will take this week given recent high refinery run rates and strong demand.

Gasoline supply and demand have been in near balance, with output at 8.233 million barrels a day (bpd), according to the latest American Petroleum Institute data. The implied demand is at about 8.4 million bpd.
"There's just too much crude oil, and refineries are running it through at nearly full capacity," said an East Coast trader.
Another East Coast player said there appeared to be little chance for a recovery in products prices in the nearterm because of the strong refinery output across the U.S.
Some traders hope however, that the high level of refinery runs will lead to production problems, cut output and put upward pressure on prices.
But other warn that may not be a good trading strategy.
"The price of betting that some refinery will go bang is very expensive ... and it hasn't made anyone rich in the past 15 years," according to the trader.
The direction of unleaded gasoline differentials in the Midcontinent seemed more sure-footed than in the East Coast.
Traders said differentials were likely expand this week because of a 9-day delay in deliveries into the Midwest by the Explorer Pipeline.
"I wouldn't be surprised if the basis (differential) moved up another 0.75 cent by the end of the month," said one Group player.
The delay on the Houston to Chicago pipeline stems from maintenance in April.
